scenario.speaker: marcus
scenario.briefing:
Remember TrailTonic — the functional-beverage client whose survey proposal we won back in your first week? Their study is finally green-lit, but the account team is buried under two other fieldings, so Dana volunteered us for a favor: **assemble TrailTonic's brand-perception questionnaire** from the question bank their analyst drafted.

Here's the thing about surveys that makes this job matter: once an instrument goes into field, every flaw in it is permanent. A leading question biases every single response it collects. A missing demographic can never be back-filled. **A bad instrument can't be fixed in analysis** — so the fixing happens now, at your desk.

The bank has more questions than the survey can hold, and not all of them deserve to survive. For each section, pick the questions that measure what TrailTonic's objectives actually call for — and watch the order of thought in the awareness section. The Guides cover the fundamentals; TrailTonic's measurement objectives are attached to my memo in the Inbox.

Build it like it's going to 1,200 respondents tomorrow. Because it is.

inbox.subject: Favor for the TrailTonic team — assemble their survey
inbox.body:
The TrailTonic engagement we won in round one is going into field, and their account team is stretched across two other projects. Dana offered them our help, which means I'm offering them *your* help.

The job: their analyst drafted a bank of candidate questions — more than the questionnaire can hold. You choose which ones make the final instrument. Four sections: the introduction, the awareness block, the brand-attribute block, and demographics.

A few ground rules before you start:

1. **The survey is a funnel.** General before specific, and in awareness measurement, *unaided always comes before aided* — show a respondent a brand list and you've contaminated their recall forever.
2. **Read every question out loud in your head.** If it argues for the brand, asks two things at once, or leaves you unsure what a respondent would even be answering, it doesn't ship.
3. **Demographics are a budget, not a buffet.** The client allows five demographic questions. Every one must map to an objective — the recap I've attached tells you exactly which cuts the board wants.

One more time, because it's the whole lesson of this round: a bad instrument can't be fixed in analysis. Get it right before it fields.

— Marcus

attachments.title: TrailTonic — Measurement Objectives Recap
attachments.body:
**TrailTonic, Inc. — Brand-Perception Study: Measurement Objectives**

*Prepared for the survey-design phase. Summarizes the objectives from TrailTonic's original RFP.*

**Business decision.** TrailTonic's board must allocate next year's marketing budget between brand-building and performance channels. The allocation depends on where the brand stands today with its target market.

**Target population.** U.S. adults who exercise outdoors at least weekly (trail running, hiking, climbing, paddling, cycling). Results must be projectable to this population — findings go to the board, so measurement precision matters more than depth.

**What the instrument must measure:**

1. **Unaided and aided awareness** of TrailTonic relative to competing functional-beverage brands. Unaided recall must be captured before any brand list is shown.
2. **Brand perceptions** on the attributes the board tracks: taste, efficacy, value for money, and packaging.
3. **Brand preference** within the competitive set.
4. **Differences across segments.** The board specifically wants results cut by **age group**, **region**, and **category usage** (frequency of outdoor exercise), with **household income** available for the value-perception analysis.

**Instrument constraints.** Target length under 10 minutes. Responses are anonymous — no personally identifying information may be collected. A maximum of **five demographic questions** is permitted.

**Contact.** J. Meade, CMO, TrailTonic, Inc.

pages.title: Assemble TrailTonic's Brand-Perception Survey
pages.intro: Build the questionnaire section by section. In each section, select the required number of questions from the bank. Read the full wording of every option — the flaws are in the details. TrailTonic's measurement objectives are attached to Marcus's memo in the Inbox.

tasks.title: TrailTonic Brand-Perception Survey
tasks.prompt: Assemble the final instrument: one introduction, two awareness questions, two brand-attribute questions, and five demographic questions. Every choice should trace back to TrailTonic's measurement objectives.

sections.label: Survey Introduction
sections.note: Select the 1 introduction that follows best practice.

options.label: Neutral introduction with purpose, length, and anonymity
options.text: Thank you for taking part in this study. We are an independent research firm studying beverages made for outdoor activities. The questionnaire takes about 7 minutes. Your answers are anonymous and will be reported only in combination with other responses. There are no right or wrong answers — we are interested in your honest opinions. You may skip any question or stop at any time.

options.label: Brand-cheerleading introduction
options.text: TrailTonic is the fastest-growing beverage on the trail, and we need your help to prove TrailTonic is the best. Please keep TrailTonic in mind as you answer the following questions so we can show the board how strong the brand really is.

options.label: Curt instruction-only introduction
options.text: Answer all of the questions below. Do not skip any question. The survey will not submit unless every item is complete.

sections.label: Awareness Block
sections.note: Select the 2 questions that establish category and brand awareness — in the right order of thought.

options.label: Unaided brand recall (open-ended)
options.text: When you think of beverages made for outdoor exercise — trail running, hiking, climbing, paddling — which brands come to mind? Please list every brand you can think of.

options.label: Aided brand awareness (brand list)
options.text: Which of the following brands of outdoor performance beverages have you heard of, even if only by name? Select all that apply.

options.label: Awareness question with a built-in endorsement
options.text: TrailTonic has been winning fans at trailheads across the country — you have probably seen it out there. Do you recognize the TrailTonic name?

options.label: Awareness-plus-purchase question
options.text: Have you heard of TrailTonic and purchased it in the past month?

sections.label: Brand-Attribute Block
sections.note: Select the 2 questions that measure the brand perceptions the board tracks.

options.label: Attribute rating matrix (1–5)
options.text: Please rate TrailTonic on each attribute below, using a scale from 1 to 5 where 1 = poor and 5 = excellent.

options.label: Brand preference ranking (rotated brand sets)
options.text: Rank the following brands from most preferred (1) to least preferred (4), based on your overall impression. Each respondent sees one of two brand sets, rotated at random.

options.label: Vague agree/disagree item
options.text: TrailTonic is a pretty good brand that most people generally like.

options.label: 27-point overall-quality scale
options.text: Rate the overall quality of TrailTonic on a scale from 1 to 27, where 1 = abysmal, 9 = tolerable, 14 = fine, 21 = admirable, and 27 = transcendent.

sections.label: Demographics Block
sections.note: Only 5 demographic questions are permitted — pick the ones the objectives actually need.

options.label: Age band
options.text: Which of the following age groups do you fall into?

options.label: Gender
options.text: How do you describe your gender?

options.label: Region
options.text: In which region of the United States do you currently live?

options.label: Outdoor-exercise frequency
options.text: In a typical week, how often do you exercise outdoors (trail running, hiking, climbing, paddling, cycling, or similar)?

options.label: Household income
options.text: Which of the following ranges includes your total annual household income before taxes?

options.label: Religious affiliation
options.text: What is your religious affiliation?

options.label: Exact street address
options.text: Please enter your full street address, including apartment or unit number.

options.label: Number of pets
options.text: How many pets live in your household?

options.label: Favorite color
options.text: What is your favorite color?

guides.title: Survey-Building Fundamentals
guides.body:
**A questionnaire is a funnel.** It moves from general to specific, and the order protects the data:

1. **Introduction & consent** — state the purpose, the approximate length, and the anonymity of responses; tell respondents there are no right or wrong answers and that they may skip or stop. A neutral introduction earns honest answers; a brand-cheerleading one poisons everything that follows.
2. **Screener** — qualify the right respondents before wasting their time (or yours).
3. **Awareness — unaided BEFORE aided.** Ask what brands come to mind *first*, as an open-ended question. Only then show a brand list for aided awareness. Once a respondent has seen the list, an unaided read is impossible — you cannot un-ring that bell.
4. **Attitudes & attributes** — ratings, rankings, perceptions.
5. **Behavior** — purchase incidence, usage.
6. **Demographics — always last.** They feel intrusive; asking them early raises abandonment.

**The three wording sins:**

- **Leading** — the question argues for an answer ("TrailTonic has been winning fans…"). Anything that praises, presumes, or pressures biases the response.
- **Double-barreled** — two questions wearing one question's clothes ("Have you heard of X *and* purchased it?"). A Yes or a No is uninterpretable.
- **Vague quantifiers** — "pretty good," "generally," "often," "regularly." If two respondents can read the same words and answer different questions, the item is broken.

**Scale discipline.** Use 5- or 7-point scales with labeled endpoints, kept consistent in direction across the survey. Exotic scales (1 to 27, anyone?) add noise, not precision, and can't be compared to anything.

**Keep it short.** Every question costs completion rate and attention. If a question doesn't map to an objective, it doesn't make the instrument.

guides.title: Choosing Demographics Deliberately
guides.body:
Demographic questions feel free — they're short, familiar, easy to write. They are not free. Each one costs respondent goodwill, and the wrong ones cost you the study.

**The one rule: every demographic must map to a planned analysis.** Before including a question, name the cut it enables — a segment the client asked for, a quota you must monitor, a weighting variable. If you can't name the analysis, cut the question. Read the client's measurement objectives: they usually tell you *exactly* which cuts the decision-makers want.

**Category-usage questions count.** A question like exercise frequency or purchase frequency often lives in the demographics block because it classifies respondents for segmentation — if the objectives call for cuts by usage, it earns a slot.

**Handle sensitivity with intent.** Religion, political views, and precise income are sensitive topics. Include them only when an objective requires that exact cut, always with a "prefer not to say" option. A sensitive question with no analytical purpose is pure downside: it raises abandonment and buys you nothing.

**Never collect PII in an anonymous study.** Names, street addresses, phone numbers, and emails directly contradict an anonymity promise made in the introduction — and they create a data-protection liability the client did not sign up for. If the design ever genuinely needs recontact information, that is a separate, explicit opt-in — never a demographics item.

**And a final gut check:** if a question would make you hesitate to answer it at a stranger's request, your respondents will hesitate too — and many will simply leave.
